\section*{Examples}

\begin{enumerate}
\item The mean number in the system for the $M/M/1$ queue is given by considering
the expectation under the steady state distribution. Compute this
value.


\answer{


\subsection*{Answer}

\begin{eqnarray*}
\left\langle k\right\rangle _{P\left(k\right)} & = & \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}kP\left(k\right)\\
 & = & \left(1-\rho\right)\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}k\rho^{k}\\
 & = & \rho\left(1-\rho\right)\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}k\rho^{k-1}\\
 & = & \rho\left(1-\rho\right)\frac{\partial\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\rho^{k}}{\partial\rho}\\
 & = & \rho\left(1-\rho\right)\frac{\partial}{\partial\rho}\left[\frac{1}{1-\rho}\right]\\
 & = & \rho\left(1-\rho\right)\frac{1}{\left(1-\rho\right)^{2}}\\
 & = & \frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\\
 & = & \frac{\lambda}{\mu-\lambda}\end{eqnarray*}


}{0}

\end{enumerate}

\chapter{Little's Formula}

In the last chapter we introduced birth-death processes and demonstrated
how we could compute the average number in the system for the stationary
distribution. An important quality of service issue is the average
delay associated with the system. We would also like to be able to
compute the average number in the queue and the average time spent
queueing (as opposed to queueing and being served).

In this chapter we introduce Little's formula, a very general formula
which can be applied to $G/G/1$ queues. It gives the relationship
between the steady-state average number of customers in the system,
$\bar{N}$, the steady-state arrival rate, $\lambda$, and the steady-state
customer delay, $\bar{T}$. First of all we will introduce a new type
of average, the time based average, then we introduce Little's formula
and review a simple derivation of the formula which highlights the
conditions under which it applies. 


\section{Time and Steady State Averages}

We have already introduced the concept of distribution means and sample
based means. In this section we introduce a further type of average,
a time based average. The time average is the average value of a particular
function over time. If that function is continuous it is given by\[
\bar{f}_{t}=\frac{1}{t}\int_{0}^{t}f\left(\tau\right)d\tau.\]
The derivation of Little's formula that follows will rely on an assumption.
We will assume that averages under the steady state distribution are
equivalent to the time average in the limit as $t\rightarrow\infty$,
where if the state of the system is given as a function of time as
$N\left(t\right)$ the average number in the system as a function
of time is given by \[
\bar{N}_{t}=\frac{1}{t}\int_{0}^{t}N\left(\tau\right)d\tau\]
and the time average after in the limit as $t\rightarrow\infty$ is
given by \[
\bar{N}=\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\bar{N}\left(t\right).\]
which we assume is equivalent to $\left\langle k\right\rangle _{p\left(k\right)}\equiv\bar{N}$.
See pg 156-157 in \cite{Bertsekas:data92} for more details. 


\section{The Formula}

Little's formula applies under steady state conditions (see Section~\ref{sec:steadyState}).
Under the steady state assumptions it states,\[
\bar{N}=\lambda\bar{T}.\]
In practice we can see what this means by considering a simple example
of a nightclub queue.


\subsubsection*{Question}

You are driving past a nightclub, wondering how long you will have
to wait to go in. You notice on Thursday nights that the queue typically
contains 20 people and that people arrive at a rate of 40 per hour. 

According to Little's formula, how long would you expect to have to
wait to get in? 


\subsubsection*{Answer}

The waiting time is given by Little's formula. $\bar{N}=20$, $\lambda=40$
and $\bar{T}=\frac{\bar{N}}{\lambda}=\frac{20}{40}=\frac{1}{2}\textrm{hour}$. 


\subsection{Intuition}

When phrased in these terms the formula seems fairly obvious. If we
see there are twenty people in a queue and they enter a building at
a rate of 40 per hour, we might expect to have to wait half-an-hour
in the queue. In the examples section at the end of this chapter we
build on this intuition with a simple graphical `proof' of the formula
based upon that given in \cite{Bertsekas:data92}. 

The formula applies regardless of the arrival and service time distributions,
it only relies on the system being in steady state. Little's formula
can be used at the level of the entire system (queueing time and service
time), as we have seen, or it may be applied at a lower level. 


\section{Average Delay in $M/M/1$}

In the last chapter we computed that the average state of an $M/M/1$
queue was given by\[
\bar{N}=\frac{\lambda}{\mu-\lambda}=\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}.\]
We can use Little's formula to tell us the average delay associated
with the system. From $\bar{N}=\lambda\bar{T}$ we rearrange to recover
the average delay as\[
\bar{T}=\frac{1}{\mu-\lambda}\]
 This is not the time spent in the queue however, this is the time
spent in the system which includes \emph{propagation delay}, the delay
in transmitting the packet. 


\subsection{Little's Formula for Queueing Time and Transmission Time }

The total delay for packet switching systems can be divided into queueing
time, $W$, and service time or transmission time, $X$. $T=X+W.$
Similarly the average delay may be decomposed as\[
\bar{T}=\bar{X}+\bar{W}.\]
 Furthermore, both the queue itself and the transmission may the be
analysed independently using Little's formula. 


\subsection{The Transmission}

If we assume that customers/packets do not leave the queue then the
rate of arrivals at the queue must equal the rate of arrivals at transmission.
If we define the the average number under transmission as $\rho$
then we can write\[
\rho=\lambda\bar{X},\]
where $\bar{X}$ is the average time spend under transmission for
each packet. For the $M/M/1$ queue the average transmission time
is given by the mean of an exponential distribution, $\bar{X}=\frac{1}{\mu}$,
so for the $M/M/1$ queue we have\[
\rho=\frac{\lambda}{\mu},\]
 a formula which we have already used in the last chapter. 

The variable $\rho$ is known as the utilisation factor. It represents
the fraction of time that the transmission line (or server) is in
use and is therefore a measure of efficiency. Note that it is also
the steady state probability that the transmission line is in use.
For a lossless system (one that doesn't drop packets) this probability
is given by $1-P\left(0\right)$. You can check that this is consistent
for the $M/M/1$ by looking at equation (\ref{eq:MM1emptyProb}).

\emph{Note}: time under transmission is often considered proportional
to packet length. For packet length of $L$ bits and bandwidth of
$C$ bits per second transmission time is $X=\frac{L}{C}$. 


\subsection{The Queue}

Given $\lambda$, an arrival rate, $\bar{N}_{Q}$, the average number
of packets waiting in the queue, and $\bar{W}$, the average packet
waiting time, Little's formula gives \[
\bar{N}_{Q}=\lambda\bar{W}\]
for the number in the queue. For the $M/M/1$ queue $\bar{T}=\bar{X}+\bar{W}=\frac{1}{\mu}+\bar{W}$
so the average time spent waiting in the queue is given by\[
\bar{W}=\bar{T}-\frac{1}{\mu}=\frac{\rho}{\mu-\lambda}.\]
We can therefore recover the average number in the queue\[
\bar{N}_{Q}=\frac{\rho^{2}}{1-\rho}.\]
 


\section*{Examples}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Graphical Proof of Little's Formula.} In this example we provide
a graphical proof of Little's formula.\answer{


\subsubsection*{Answer}

First we sketch two curves, the number of arrivals ($\alpha\left(\tau\right)$)
and the number of departures ($\beta\left(\tau\right)$) from a queue
vs time.

%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\includegraphics[%
  width=0.60\textwidth]{./diagrams/littlesFormula.eps}\end{center}


\caption{Graphical `proof' of Little's formula.\label{cap:littlesGraphical}}
\end{figure}


By looking at Figure~\ref{cap:littlesGraphical} we note that the
area between the lines in the top figure can be expressed as both
$\int_{0}^{t}N(\tau)d\tau$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{\alpha\left(t\right)}T_{i}$.
We may therefore equate these expressions,\[
\int_{0}^{t}N\left(\tau\right)d\tau=\sum_{i=1}^{\alpha(t)}T_{i},\]
we then introduce the number of arrivals on the right hand side,\[
\int_{0}^{t}N\left(\tau\right)d\tau=\alpha\left(t\right)\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{\alpha\left(t\right)}T_{i}}{\alpha\left(t\right)}\]
and divide both sides by $t$,\[
\frac{1}{t}\int_{0}^{t}N\left(\tau\right)d\tau=\frac{\alpha\left(t\right)}{t}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{\alpha\left(t\right)}T_{i}}{\alpha\left(t\right)}.\]
The equation now has the form of three averages. The term on the left
hand side of the equation is an average, over time, of the number
in the system. This average is a function of time and we write it
\[
\bar{N}_{t}=\frac{1}{t}\int_{0}^{t}N\left(\tau\right).\]
We also note that the right hand side of the equation is also composed
of two averages: \[
\bar{\lambda}_{t}=\frac{\alpha\left(t\right)}{t},\]
is the average of the arrivals over time and \[
\bar{T}_{t}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{\alpha\left(t\right)}T_{i}}{\alpha\left(t\right)}\]
 is the average waiting time. So we write\[
\bar{N}_{t}=\bar{\lambda}_{t}\bar{T}_{t}.\]
Dividing both expressions by $t$, equating them, and taking the limit
as $t\rightarrow\infty$ gives Little's formula. We wish to consider
the steady state behaviour. The system may not have steady state behaviour.
If the steady state exists, we can seek it in the limit as $t\rightarrow\infty$,
giving \[
\bar{N}=\lambda\bar{T}\]
}{0}

\item \textbf{Simple example of Little's formula}. You are at a queue in
a bar, and notice that the bar tender spends 10\% of her time cleaning
between serving customers. If the typical number of people waiting
to be served is $3$, what is the ratio of time spent waiting to being
served? \answer{


\subsubsection*{Answer}

Information says $\rho=0.9$ and $\bar{N}_{Q}=3$. \[
\lambda=\frac{0.9}{\bar{X}}.\]


\[
3=\lambda\bar{W}.\]


Therefore $\frac{\bar{W}}{\bar{X}}=3\frac{1}{3}$. }{0}

\end{enumerate}

\chapter{Other Markov Queues}

We have already met the $M/M/1$ queue, the simplest Markov queue.
In this chapter we will introduce related Markov queues and compute
their stationary distributions. The simplest modifications to the
$M/M/1$ queue are given by a \emph{finite length} modification which
we write in Kendall's notation as $M/M/1/m$ and the \emph{infinite
server} queue\emph{,} $M/M/\infty$. 


\section{Finite Length $M$/$M$/$1$/$m$}

In our analysis of the $M/M/1$ queue so far we have assumed that
the queue can have an infinite length, in practice a restricted buffer
size may mean that the queue length is also restricted. Let's assume
the queue can contain at maximum $m$ customers (as shown in Figure~\ref{cap:stateDiagramMM1m}),
we can now derive the stationary distribution for this queue.

%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\includegraphics[%
  width=1.0\textwidth]{diagrams/stateMM1m.eps}\end{center}


\caption{State diagram for the $M/M/1/m$ queue. Note that there are no transitions
to states above the $m$th state.\label{cap:stateDiagramMM1m}}
\end{figure}
 


\subsection{Balance Equation}

The balance equation for the $M/M/1/m$ is identical to that for the
$M/M/1$ (Section~\ref{sec:MM1Stationary}). The first step is to
draw the flow rates at the boundary (Figure~\ref{cap:flowAtBoundaryMM1m}).

%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\includegraphics[%
  width=0.40\textwidth]{./diagrams/boundaryFlowMM1.eps}\end{center}


\caption{Flow rates at a boundary for the $M/M/1/m$ queue.\label{cap:flowAtBoundaryMM1m}}
\end{figure}
At steady state, the expected flow from $k-1$ to $k$ is given by
$\lambda P\left(k-1\right)$. Flow from $k$ to $k-1$ is given $\mu P\left(k-1\right)$.
For flow to be balanced we have \[
\lambda P\left(k-1\right)=\mu P\left(k\right)\]
 leading to \[
P\left(k\right)=\frac{\lambda}{\mu}P\left(k-1\right).\]
Substituting into the detailed balance equation we get\[
P\left(k\right)=\frac{\lambda}{\mu}P\left(k-1\right)\]
 Thus \begin{eqnarray*}
P\left(k\right) & = & \left(\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\right)^{k}P\left(0\right)\\
 & = & \rho^{k}P\left(0\right).\end{eqnarray*}
 


\subsection{Normalisation}

In the case of the finite length queue the normalisation is computed
with a sum over only $m$ states, rather than $\infty$ states. This
leads to a different value for $P\left(0\right)$. We compute $P\left(0\right)$
by writing the sum across all the $m+1$ states of the distribution,
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{m}P\left(0\right)\rho^{k}=1.\]
This leads us to \[
P\left(0\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{m}\frac{1}{\rho^{k}}\]
which is recognised as the \emph{finite} sum of a geometric series,\[
\sum_{k=0}^{m}\frac{1}{\rho^{k}}=\frac{1-\rho}{1-\rho^{m+1}}\]
so we have\[
P\left(0\right)=\frac{1-\rho}{1-\rho^{m+1}}\]
which leads to \[
P\left(k\right)=\frac{\rho^{k}\left(1-\rho\right)}{1-\rho^{m+1}}.\]



\subsubsection{Example --- Blocking Probabilities}


\subsubsection*{Question}

Given a finite length $M$/$M$/$1$/$m$ queue, what is the probability
that an arrival is blocked from joining the queue (and therefore lost). 


\subsubsection*{Answer}

\answer{This is answered by determining the probability of the queue
being full, which means \[
P\left(m\right)=\frac{\rho^{m}\left(1-\rho\right)}{1-\rho^{m+1}}\]
}{6}

The $M/M/1/m$ queue covers the case where the queue length is bounded.
Another queue that is straightforward to derive is where the number
of servers is \emph{unbounded}.


\section{Infinite Serving Capacity --- $M$/$M$/$\infty$}

In the $M/M/1$ queue we assume that there is only one server. In
some cases it can be useful to consider an unlimited number of servers
so that there is one server for every customer in the system. The
state diagram for this system can be drawn as in Figure~\ref{cap:stateDiagramMMinf}
%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\answer{\includegraphics[%
  width=1.0\textwidth]{diagrams/stateMMinf.eps}}{6}\end{center}


\caption{State diagram for the $M/M/\infty$ queue. \label{cap:stateDiagramMMinf}}
\end{figure}
 


\subsection{Detailed Balance }

We again make use of the standard detailed balance equations for this
queue, from the flow rates at the boundary we have in general

\[
\lambda_{k-1}P\left(k-1\right)=\mu_{k}P\left(k\right)\]
Since there is infinite service capacity in the queue the service
rate at state $k$ is simply $\mu_{k}=k\mu$. The rate of arrivals
stays constant, $\lambda_{k}=\lambda$, so for this queue detailed
balance gives.\[
\lambda P\left(k-1\right)=k\mu P\left(k\right)\]
%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\answer{\includegraphics[%
  width=0.60\textwidth]{./diagrams/boundaryFlowMMinf.eps}}{6}\end{center}


\caption{Flow rates at a boundary for $M/M/\infty$ queue.\label{cap:flowAtBoundaryMMinf}}
\end{figure}
Reorganising in terms of $P\left(k\right)$ then gives\[
P\left(k\right)=\frac{\lambda}{k\mu}P\left(k-1\right)\]
and therefore\[
P\left(k\right)=P\left(0\right)\left(\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\right)^{k}\frac{1}{k!}.\]



\subsection{Normalisation Condition}

Using the normalisation condition for this queue, \[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}P\left(k\right)=1,\]
we obtain $P\left(0\right)$ as \begin{equation}
P\left(0\right)=\left[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\right)^{k}\frac{1}{k!}\right]^{-1}.\label{eq:MMinftyP0}\end{equation}



\subsubsection{The Offered Load\label{sub:offeredLoad}}

It is convenient in this (and later queues) to define the offered
load, $a=\frac{\lambda}{\mu}$, as arrival rate divided by service
rate. This is a dimensionless constant, but has international standard
units of Erlangs (after A.~K.~Erlang). Substituting this definition
back into (\ref{eq:MMinftyP0}) we have, \[
P\left(0\right)=\left[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{a^{k}}{k!}\right]^{-1}.\]
Recalling from Section~\ref{sub:poissonMeanVar} that \[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{n}}{n!}=\exp\left(x\right)\]
 we have\[
P\left(0\right)=\exp\left(-a\right)\]
and the steady state distribution is then\[
P\left(k\right)=\frac{a^{k}}{k!}\exp\left(-a\right)\]
which is recognised as a Poisson distribution with parameter $a$.
Notice that the utilization factor for this queue, $\rho$, is \emph{not}
equal to $\frac{\lambda}{\mu}$ which is refered to as the offered
load. In fact for the $M/M/\infty$ queue the offered load can be
much larger than 1 but we know that the utilization factor is never
greater than $1$. The utilization factor for this queue can be seen
to be \[
1-P\left(0\right)=1-\exp\left(-a\right).\]



\chapter{Erlang Delay $M$/$M$/$m$ }

In the last chapter we considered the situation were there are as
many servers as there are customers. More realistic real world situations
involve limited numbers of servers. This commonly arises in, for example,
call centres. This system is known as the \emph{Erlang delay} system.
In Kendall's notation it is written $M/M/m$.


\section{Stationary Distribution}

In the context of the Erlang delay system it is ususal to refer to
the `average holding time', $\tau=\frac{1}{\mu}\equiv\bar{X}$, which,
for a network involving telephones, would be the time a call is open.

We give a schemeatic overview of an Erlang delay system in Figure~\ref{cap:erlangDelaySchematic}.

{\small }%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\answer{\includegraphics[%
  width=0.80\textwidth]{diagrams/erlangDelayDiagram.eps}}{6}\end{center}


\caption{Queueing model of the Erlang delay system.\label{cap:erlangDelaySchematic}}
\end{figure}
{\small \par}


\subsection{State Diagram}

As with all the Markov based systems we have met so far the first
step in their analysis is to write down their state diagram.

{\tiny }%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\includegraphics[%
  width=1.0\textwidth]{diagrams/erlangDelay.eps}\end{center}


\caption{State diagram of an Erlang delay system.}
\end{figure}
The Erlang loss system may be analysed as a birth-death process with
birth rate \[
\lambda_{k}=\lambda\]
 and death rate \[
\mu_{k}=\left\{ \begin{array}{cc}
k\mu & k=0,1,\dots,m-1\\
m\mu & k>m\end{array}\right.\]



\subsection{Detailed Balance Equations}

The `death rate' $\mu_{k}$ has different definitions for different
parts of the state space. To derive the detailed balance equation
we need to consider detailed balance for each part in turn,


\subsubsection*{$k\leq m$}

When the system's state, $k$, is less than or equal to the number
of servers we have boundary flow as in Figure~\ref{cap:flowAtBoundaryMMma},%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\answer{\includegraphics[%
  width=0.60\textwidth]{./diagrams/boundaryFlowMMinf.eps}}{6}\end{center}


\caption{Flow rates at a boundary.\label{cap:flowAtBoundaryMMma}}
\end{figure}
which leads to the following balance equation \[
\lambda P\left(k-1\right)=k\mu P\left(k\right).\]
As a result, for $k=0\dots m$ we may write\begin{equation}
P\left(k\right)=\frac{\lambda}{k\mu}P\left(k-1\right).\label{eq:PkForPartA}\end{equation}
It will prove convenient to define \[
\rho=\frac{\lambda}{m\mu}\]
which in turn gives \[
\frac{\lambda}{k\mu}=\frac{m\rho}{k}\]
which we substitute back into (\ref{eq:PkForPartA}) obtaining\[
P\left(k\right)=\frac{m\rho}{k}P\left(k-1\right)\]
and as before\begin{eqnarray}
P\left(k\right)=\frac{\left(m\rho\right)^{k}}{k!}P\left(0\right) & \textrm{for} & k\leq m\label{eq:probabilities}\end{eqnarray}



\subsubsection*{$k>m$}

When the system's state is greater than $m$, $k>m$ the flow at the
boundary is as in Figure~\ref{cap:flowAtBoundaryMMmb}, the detailed
balance equation is then%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\answer{\includegraphics[%
  width=0.60\textwidth]{./diagrams/boundaryFlowMMm.eps}}{6}\end{center}


\caption{Flow rates at a boundary.\label{cap:flowAtBoundaryMMmb}}
\end{figure}
which leads to \[
\lambda P(k-1)=m\mu P\left(k\right)\]
therefore for $k=m+1\dots\infty$ we may write\[
P\left(k\right)=\frac{\lambda}{m\mu}P\left(k-1\right)\]
using $\rho=\frac{\lambda}{m\mu}$ we then have\[
P\left(k\right)=\rho P\left(k-1\right)\]
leading to \[
P\left(k\right)=\rho^{k-m}P\left(m\right).\]
Finally we use (\ref{eq:probabilities}) and substitute $k$ with
$m$ to find $P\left(m\right)$ which leads to\[
P\left(m\right)=\frac{\left(m\rho\right)^{m}}{m!}P\left(0\right)\]
therefore \begin{eqnarray*}
P\left(k\right)=\frac{m^{m}\rho^{k}}{m!}P\left(0\right) & \textrm{for} & k>m\end{eqnarray*}
thus we can write\[
P\left(k\right)=\left\{ \begin{array}{cc}
P\left(0\right)\frac{(m\rho)^{k}}{k!}, & k\leq m\\
P\left(0\right)\frac{m^{m}\rho^{k}}{m!} & k>m\end{array}\right.\]



\subsection{Normalisation Condition}

Once again we can compute $P\left(0\right)$ through normalisation\begin{eqnarray*}
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}P\left(k\right) & = & 1\\
P\left(0\right)\left[\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{\left(m\rho\right)^{k}}{k!}+\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\frac{m^{m}\rho^{k}}{m!}\right] & = & 1\\
P\left(0\right) & = & \left[\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{\left(m\rho\right)^{k}}{k!}+\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\frac{m^{m}\rho^{k}}{m!}\right]^{-1}.\end{eqnarray*}
Consider the second term inside the bracket,\[
\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\frac{m^{m}}{m!}\rho^{k}=\frac{m^{m}\rho^{m}}{m!}\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\rho^{k-m}\]
substitute in $k^{\prime}=k-m$ and we obtain\[
\frac{m^{m}\rho^{m}}{m!}\sum_{k^{\prime}=0}^{\infty}\rho^{k^{\prime}}=\frac{m^{m}\rho^{m}}{m!}\frac{1}{1-\rho}\]
because, as we saw in Section~\ref{sec:MM1Stationary} \[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\rho^{k}=\frac{1}{1-\rho}\]
 if $\rho<1$. Thus we have\[
P\left(0\right)=\left[\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{\left(m\rho\right)^{k}}{k!}+\frac{m^{m}\rho^{m}}{m!\left(1-\rho\right)}\right]^{-1}.\]
Note that this relies on $\rho<1$, if $\lambda\geq m\mu$ the system
has no stationary distribution.


\section{Probability of Waiting}

For the $M/M/m$ queue a key quantity of interest is the probability
of of a customer queueing, $P_{Q}$. What is the probability, when
the system is at steady state, that a customer will arrive and find
all the $m$ servers busy? \[
P\left(k\geq m\right)=\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}P\left(k\right)=P\left(0\right)\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\frac{m^{m}\rho^{k}}{m!}=P\left(0\right)\frac{\left(\rho m\right)^{m}}{m!}\sum_{k=m}^{\infty}\rho^{k-m}\doteq C\left(m,a\right),\]
making the same substitution as above this can be re-written\begin{equation}
C\left(m,a\right)=P\left(0\right)\frac{\left(\rho m\right)^{m}}{m!\left(1-\rho\right)}.\label{eq:ErlangCone}\end{equation}
This is known as the \emph{Erlang C formula}, or Erlang's second formula
after A.K. Erlang a pioneer of queueing theory. By making use of our
definition of, $a$, (from Section~\ref{sub:offeredLoad}) the offered
load can be written\[
a=\frac{\lambda}{\mu}=m\rho\]
 and substituting into (\ref{eq:ErlangCone}) we have \[
C(m,a)=\frac{P\left(0\right)a^{m}}{m!\left(1-\frac{a}{m}\right)}.\]
Nowadays we can compute the result of this formula on a computer,
however for the purposes of exams and exercises we will use the old
fashioned method of curves.


\section{Erlang C Curves}

In your notes we provide you with two sets of curves in Figure~\ref{cap:erlangCOne}
and \ref{cap:erlangCTwo}. In an exam, if there were

\subsubsection*{Question}

\begin{enumerate}
\item Consider the telephone trunking problem. A telephone exchange A is
to server 10,000 subscribers in a nearby exchange as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:exchange}.

\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\includegraphics[%
  width=0.80\textwidth]{diagrams/exchange.eps}\end{center}


\caption{The telephone exchange.\label{fig:exchange}}
\end{figure}
Suppose that during the busy hour, the subscribers generate a Poisson
traffic with a rate of 10 calls per minute, which requires trunk lines
to exchange B for an average holding time of 3 minutes per call. Determine
the number of trunk lines needed for a grade of service (probability

\item A customer service centre has an average holding time, $\tau$, for
calls of 8 minutes. In the busy hour, calls arrive at the centre at

From the Erlang C curves in Figure~\ref{cap:erlangCOne} it looks

\item Average call rage is $\lambda=0.5$ calls/minute. Average holding

\subsection{Average number in System.}

We can also compute the average number of calls in the Erlang Delay
System, 

\[
\bar{N}=\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}C(m,a)+m\rho\]
 These terms represent the average queue length and the average number
of busy lines. \[
\bar{N}_{Q}=\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}C(m,a)\]
 So the average waiting time is simply \[
\bar{W}=\frac{\bar{N}_{Q}}{\lambda}=\frac{C(m,a)}{m\mu(1-\rho)}\]



\subsubsection*{Question}

So what is the average waiting time for the telephone service centre
example? 


\subsubsection*{Answer}

\answer{$m=8$, $\mu=\frac{1}{8}$, $\rho=\frac{\lambda}{m\mu}=\frac{1}{2}$
delay is $\frac{0.1}{8\frac{1}{8}\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)}=0.2$
minutes, or 12 seconds. }{5}


\chapter{Erlang Loss $M$/$M$/$m$/$m$}

The Erlang delay system contained $m$ servers, and it was assumed
that, if all servers were occupied, the customer would be placed on
hold until a server became available. In the $M/M/m/m$ system there
is a finite number of customers. 

%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\includegraphics[%
  width=0.80\textwidth]{diagrams/erlangLossFlowChart.eps}\end{center}


\caption{Flow chart of the Erlang Loss System.\label{cap:erlangLossFlowChart}}
\end{figure}


The system is shown as a flow chart in Figure~\ref{cap:erlangLossFlowChart}The
Erlang loss system may be analysed as a birth-death process with birth
rate \[
\lambda_{k}=\left\{ \begin{array}{cc}
\lambda & k=0,1,\dots,m-1\\
0 & k\geq m\end{array}\right.\]
 and death rate \[
\mu_{k}=\left\{ \begin{array}{cc}
k\mu & k=0,1,\dots,m\\
0 & k>m\end{array}\right.\]
 {[}\emph{Note: for the lower line, it doesn't matter what $\mu_{k}$
is.}{]} 

{\tiny }%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\includegraphics[%
  width=1.0\textwidth]{./diagrams/erlangLoss.eps}\end{center}


\caption{Markov chain for the Erlang loss system, $M$/$M$/$m$/$m$}
\end{figure}
{\tiny \par}

The offered load, $a=\frac{\lambda}{\mu}$, is again dimensionless
with units of Erlangs. 


\subsection{Steady State Probabilities}

Using the detailed balance equations we find \begin{eqnarray*}
P\left(k\right) & = & \frac{\lambda_{k}}{\mu_{k}}P(k-1)\\
 & = & \frac{\lambda}{k\mu}P(k-1)\\
 & = & \frac{a}{k}P(k-1)\end{eqnarray*}
 Which means that \begin{eqnarray*}
P\left(k\right) & = & \prod_{n=1}^{k}\frac{a}{n}P\left(0\right)\\
 & = & \frac{a^{k}}{k!}P\left(0\right)\end{eqnarray*}
 The normalisation condition gives us \[
P\left(0\right)\sum_{k=0}^{m}\frac{a^{k}}{k!}=1\]
\[
P\left(0\right)=\frac{1}{\sum_{k=0}^{m}\frac{a^{k}}{k!}}\]
 which leads to the truncated Poisson distribution \[
P\left(k\right)=\frac{\frac{a^{k}}{k!}}{\sum_{n=0}^{m}\frac{a^{n}}{n!}}\]
 Note if $m\rightarrow\infty$ we recover the $M/M/\infty$ queue
as we would expect.


\subsection{Performance Measures for Erlang B}

For the blocking probability and the Erlang B curves we are interested
in the probability that when we arrive the queue is full \[
B(m,a)=P\left(m\right)=\frac{\frac{a^{m}}{m!}}{\sum_{n=0}^{m}\frac{a^{n}}{n!}}\]
 {\small }%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\includegraphics[%
  width=1.0\textwidth]{diagrams/erlangBCurves0to20.eps}\end{center}


\caption{Erlang B curves.}
\end{figure}
{\small \par}

{\small }%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\includegraphics[%
  width=1.0\textwidth]{diagrams/erlangBCurves0to100.eps}\end{center}


\caption{Erlang B curves.}
\end{figure}
{\small \par}


\subsection{Carried Load}

Since traffic is lost in $M/M/m/m$ the carried load, $a^{\prime}$,
is smaller than the offered load. It may be found as \[
a^{\prime}=a(1-P\left(m\right))=a(1-B(m,a))\]
 The carried load per line is the trunk occupancy, \[
\rho=\frac{a^{\prime}}{m},\]
 or the utilization factor --- it is a measure of efficiency of the
line. Note the contrast with the lossless systems where \[
\rho=\frac{a}{m}\]
because $a^{\prime}=a$. 


\subsection{Example Load tripling.}


\subsubsection*{Question}

\begin{enumerate}
\item For a blocking probability of 0.01, what is the number of trunks needed
for 6 Erlangs of offered load?
\item For a blocking probability of 0.01, what is the number of trunks needed
for 18 Erlangs?
\item Comment on the increase in load compared to the increase in the number
of trunks. 
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection*{Answer}

\answer{

\begin{enumerate}
\item 12
\item 28
\item A load increase of 200 \% only lead to a trunk increase of 133 \%.
To understand this further we look at the utilization factors. For
the first system the utilisation factor is \[
\rho_{1}=\frac{6}{12}\left(1-0.01\right)=0.495\]
whereas for the second system the utilisation factor is\[
\rho_{2}=\frac{18}{28}\left(1-0.007\right)=0.6384\]
The 30 trunk system is thus more efficient. This explains why it is
cheaper to call the U.S.A. than Italy.
\end{enumerate}
}{8}

\chapter{$M$/$G$/$1$ Queue}


\section{Pollaczek-Khinchin formula}

If service times are general we cannot use birth death processes to
analyse the system. 

Instead we derive the Pollaczek-Khinchin formula. This formula gives
an expression for the expected waiting time in the queue for any distribution
of service times. \[
\bar{W}=\frac{\lambda\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle }{2(1-\rho)}\]
 where $\bar{W}$ is expected waiting time, $\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle =\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle _{p(X)}$,
$\rho=\lambda\bar{X}$ and $\bar{X}=\left\langle X\right\rangle _{p(X)}$. 


\section{Proof of Pollaczek-Khinchin Formula}

We assume that we have a FIFO queue, \emph{i.e.} customers are served
in the order they arrive. We also assume that arrival times are independent
of service times. We will use a new concept known as Mean Residual
Service Time. 


\section{The Residual Service Time}

Some definitions: 

\begin{tabular}{rcl}
 $W_{i}$&
=&
 Waiting time in queue of $i$th customer.\tabularnewline
 $R_{i}$&
=&
 `Residual service time' seen by the $i$th customer.\tabularnewline
 $X_{i}$&
=&
 Service time of the $i$th customer.\tabularnewline
 $k_{i}$&
=&
 Number of customers in the system when the $i$th customer arrives. \tabularnewline
\end{tabular}

%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\includegraphics[%
  width=0.80\textwidth]{diagrams/residualServiceOverview.eps}\end{center}


\caption{Graphical representation of residual service time.}
\end{figure}


From these definitions we may immediately write down \[
W_{i}=R_{i}+\sum_{j=i-(k_{i}-1)}^{i-1}X_{j}\]
 summing both sides across $i$ we obtain \[
\sum_{i=1}^{I}W_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{I}R_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{j=i-(k_{i}-1)}^{i-1}X_{j}\]
 dividing through by $I$ gives us \[
\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{W_{i}}{I}=\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{R_{i}}{I}+\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{j=i-(k_{i}-1)}^{i-1}\frac{X_{j}}{I}\]
 in the limit as $I\rightarrow\infty$ this becomes \[
\lim_{I\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{W_{i}}{I}=\lim_{I\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{R_{i}}{I}+\lim_{I\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{(k_{i}-1)X_{i}}{I}\]
assuming time averages are equivalent to steady state averages this
gives \[
\left\langle W\right\rangle =\left\langle R\right\rangle +\left\langle \left(k-1\right)X\right\rangle \]
 Now since the length of the queue as seen by the $i$th arrival is
independent of the $i$th arrival's length this means $\left\langle (k-1)X\right\rangle =\left\langle k-1\right\rangle \left\langle X\right\rangle $
and since $(k-1)$ is the length of the queue we may write \[
\bar{W}=\bar{R}+\bar{N}_{Q}\bar{X}\]
 Using Little's theorem \[
\bar{N}_{Q}=\lambda\bar{W}\]
 we can obtain \[
\bar{W}=\bar{R}+\lambda\bar{X}\bar{W}\]
 and the fact that $\rho=\lambda\bar{X}$ gives us \[
\bar{W}=\bar{R}+\rho\bar{W}\]
 Leading to \begin{equation}
\bar{W}=\frac{\bar{R}}{1-\rho}\label{eqn:arrivals}\end{equation}
 It remains to calculate $\bar{R}$. 


\section{Residual Service Time from Departures Perspective}

Plot of the residual service time over time. Here $M\left(t\right)$
is the number of service completions in the interval $[0,\, t]$.

%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\includegraphics[%
  width=0.80\textwidth]{diagrams/residualTime.eps}\end{center}


\caption{Graphical computation of mean residual time.}
\end{figure}


The time average of the mean residual service time can be calculated
in terms of the area under the curve, $A(t)$ which in turn is the
area under each of the triangles which may be written \[
A(t)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{M(t)}X_{i}^{2}\]
 The average service time is the area divided by time, $t$. \begin{eqnarray}
\frac{A(t)}{t} & = & \frac{M(t)}{t}\frac{A(t)}{M(t)}\\
 & = & \frac{1}{2}\frac{M(t)}{t}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{M(t)}X_{i}^{2}}{M(t)}\end{eqnarray}
 As $t\rightarrow\infty$ we find $M(t)\rightarrow\infty$ and \[
\bar{R}=\frac{1}{2}\lambda\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle .\]
 If we assume that time averages and ensemble averages are equal we
may substitute back into (\ref{eqn:arrivals}) and obtain the Pollaczek-Khinchin
formula \[
\bar{W}=\frac{\lambda\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle }{2(1-\rho)}\]


This implies that the total waiting time is \[
\bar{T}=\bar{X}+\frac{\lambda\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle }{2(1-\rho)}\]
 and through Little's formula we can obtain the expected queue length,
$\bar{N}_{Q}$, and the expected number in the system, $\bar{N}$. 

Recall that for an $M$/$M$/$1$ system the service times are exponentially
distributed,

\[
P\left(X\right)=\mu\exp\left(-\mu X\right)\]
this means that\[
\bar{X}=\frac{1}{\mu}\]
 then since the variance of the system is $\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}$\[
\left\langle X\right\rangle ^{2}=\frac{2}{\mu^{2}}\]
Substituting into the Pollaczek-Khinchin formula we obtain \begin{eqnarray*}
\bar{W} & = & \frac{\rho}{\mu\left(1-\rho\right)}\\
 & = & \frac{\rho}{\mu-\lambda}\end{eqnarray*}


Deterministic service times --- each service takes the same amount
of time\[
P\left(X\right)=\delta\left(X-\frac{1}{\mu}\right)\]
where $\delta\left(\cdot\right)$is the Dirac delta function. For
this system \[
\left\langle X\right\rangle =\frac{1}{\mu}\]
and \[
\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle =\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}\]
\emph{i.e.} the variance is zero as we would expect. Substituting
into the Pollaczek-Khinchin formula we obtain\[
\bar{W}=\frac{\rho}{2\mu\left(1-\rho\right)}\]


In fact we may derive the full range of results for these distributions. 

\begin{center}\begin{tabular}{c|c|c|c}
 Expected value &
 General &
 Exponential &
Deterministic\tabularnewline
\hline
$\bar{W}$&
 $\frac{\lambda}{2(1-\rho)}\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle $&
 $\frac{\rho}{\mu(1-\rho)}$&
 $\frac{\rho}{2\mu(1-\rho)}$\tabularnewline
 $\bar{T}=\bar{W}+\frac{1}{\mu}$&
 $\frac{\lambda}{2(1-\rho)}\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle +\frac{1}{\mu}$&
 $\frac{1}{\mu(1-\rho)}$&
 $\frac{2-\rho}{2\mu(1-\rho)}$\tabularnewline
 $\bar{N_{Q}}=\lambda\bar{W}$&
 $\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2(1-\rho)}\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle $&
$\frac{\rho^{2}}{(1-\rho)}$&
 $\frac{\rho^{2}}{2(1-\rho)}$\tabularnewline
 $\bar{N}=\lambda\bar{W}+\rho=\lambda\bar{T}$&
 $\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2(1-\rho)}\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle +\rho$&
 $\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}$&
 $\frac{\rho(2-\rho)}{2(1-\rho)}$\tabularnewline
\end{tabular}\end{center}

Uniform Service times --- A uniform probability distribution is defined
between 0 and $b$ for $X>0$ as\[
U\left(X|b\right)=\left\{ \begin{array}{cc}
\frac{1}{b} & 0<X\leq b\\
0 & X>b\end{array}\right.\]
show that the man of this uniform distribution is given by $\frac{b}{2}$
and its variance by $\frac{b^{2}}{12}$ and find the expected waiting
time for an $M/U/1$ queue?

For the mean we have\begin{eqnarray*}
\left\langle X\right\rangle  & = & \int_{0}^{\infty}Xp\left(X\right)dX\\
 & = & \int_{0}^{\infty}XU\left(X|b\right)dX\\
 & = & \int_{0}^{b}\frac{X}{b}dX\\
 & = & \left[\frac{X^{2}}{2b}\right]_{0}^{b}\\
 & = & \frac{b^{2}}{2b}-0\\
 & = & \frac{b}{2}\end{eqnarray*}
For the variance we also require \begin{eqnarray*}
\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle  & = & \int_{0}^{\infty}X^{2}p\left(X\right)dX\\
 & = & \int_{0}^{b}\frac{X^{2}}{b}dX\\
 & = & \left[\frac{X^{3}}{3b}\right]_{0}^{b}\\
 & = & \frac{b^{3}}{3b}-0\\
 & = & \frac{b^{2}}{3}\end{eqnarray*}
The variance is $\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle -\left\langle X\right\rangle ^{2}=\frac{b^{2}}{3}-\left(\frac{b}{2}\right)=\frac{b^{2}}{12}$.

\begin{description}
\item [Waiting~Time~For~Queue]For simplicity we consider $\mu=\frac{1}{\left\langle X\right\rangle }.$
So $\mu=\frac{2}{b}$ and thus $b=\frac{2}{\mu}$. So we can write
the second moment in terms of $\mu$. $\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle =\frac{b^{2}}{3}$,
substituting in $b=\frac{2}{\mu}$ we have $\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle =\frac{4}{3\mu^{2}}$.
Substituting in to the P-K formula we recover\[
\bar{W}=\frac{2\rho}{3\mu\left(1-\rho\right)}.\]

\end{description}
~


\subsubsection{Example --- Automatic Repeat Request (ARQ) System. }

%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\includegraphics[%
  width=0.80\textwidth]{diagrams/ARQ.eps}\end{center}


\caption{The ARQ System.}
\end{figure}
Assume each packet takes 1 millisecond to be transmitted.

The system waits $n-1$ milliseconds for an acknowledgment. If there
is no acknowledgment the system retransmits.

The probability of an error in a packet is taken to be $p$. Errors
are taken to be independent. Assume that packets arrive as a Poisson
process with rate $\lambda$.  Time interval between transmission
and re-transmission is $1+kn$ time units with probability $\left(1-p\right)p^{k}$

The probability of the service time is\[
P\left(X=1+kn\right)=\left(1-p\right)p^{k}\]
 The expected service time is therefore\begin{eqnarray*}
\left\langle X\right\rangle  & = & \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(1+kn\right)\left(1-p\right)p^{k}\\
 & = & \left(1-p\right)\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}p^{k}+n\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}kp^{k}\right)\\
 & = & 1+\frac{np}{1-p}\end{eqnarray*}
 since $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}p^{k}=\frac{1}{1-p}$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}kp^{k}=\frac{p}{\left(1-p\right)^{2}}$.
Thus we can write that\[
\rho=\frac{\lambda\left(1-p\right)}{1-p+np}\]
and thus \[
1-\rho=\frac{1-\lambda-p\left(n-1-\lambda\right)}{1-p+np}\]
The second moment of the service time is\begin{eqnarray*}
\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle  & = & \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left(1+kn\right)^{2}\left(1-p\right)p^{k}\\
 & = & \left(1-p\right)\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}p^{k}+2n\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}kp^{k}+n^{2}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}k^{2}p^{k}\right)\\
 & = & 1+\frac{2np}{1-p}+\frac{n^{2}\left(p+p^{2}\right)}{\left(1-p\right)^{2}}\end{eqnarray*}
since \[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}k^{2}p^{k}=\frac{p+p^{2}}{\left(1-p\right)^{3}}\]
 Substituting into the P-K formula gives a very ugly formula!


\section{$M/G/1$ Queues with Vacations }

Consider a server which, when it is free, attends to some other business,
for example it could transmit control and record keeping traffic. 

These periods are sometimes known as vacations --- American for holidays. 

\begin{itemize}
\item If a new arrival arrives during a vacation it must wait until the
vacation is over before being dealt with.
\item If a vacation ends and the server is idle it immediately goes on a
new vacation. 
\end{itemize}
~

%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\includegraphics[%
  width=0.80\textwidth]{diagrams/vacationMG1.eps}\end{center}


\caption{Schematic of $M/G/1$ queue}
\end{figure}


We denote the length of these successive vacations to be $V_{1}$,
$V_{2}$, $\dots$. 

We assume that $V_{1},$$V_{2}$, $\dots$ are i.i.d. random variables
which are also independent of the customer times and the service times. 

For a Poisson arrival system with general service times we will look
to compute the average waiting time for a system of this type. 

%
\begin{figure}[ht]
\begin{center}\includegraphics[%
  width=0.80\textwidth]{diagrams/vacationResidual.eps}\end{center}


\caption{Computation of residual service time for system with vacations.}
\end{figure}


For this system \begin{eqnarray}
\frac{1}{t}\int_{0}^{t}r\left(\tau\right)d\tau & = & \frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{M\left(t\right)}\frac{1}{2}X_{i}^{2}+\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{L\left(t\right)}\frac{1}{2}V_{i}^{2}\nonumber \\
 & = & \frac{M\left(t\right)}{t}\frac{1}{2}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{M\left(t\right)}X_{i}^{2}}{M\left(t\right)}+\frac{L\left(t\right)}{t}\frac{1}{2}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{L\left(t\right)}V_{i}^{2}}{L\left(t\right)}\label{eq:vacationResidual}\end{eqnarray}


On average the proportion of time available for utilisation is $\left(1-\rho\right)$.
If the average length of a vacation at time $t$ is $\bar{V}_{t}$
then the number of vacations that will have arrived is $L\left(t\right)=\frac{t\left(1-\rho\right)}{\bar{V}_{t}}$.
Therefore if we take the limit of (\ref{eq:vacationResidual}) as
$t\rightarrow\infty$ we find \[
\bar{R}=\frac{1}{2}\lambda\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle +\frac{\left(1-\rho\right)\left\langle V^{2}\right\rangle }{2\bar{V}}\]


So given that the assumptions that we used to develop the formula 

\[
\bar{W}=\frac{\bar{R}}{1-\rho}\]
are still valid, we may write\[
\bar{W}=\frac{\lambda\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle }{2\left(1-\rho\right)}+\frac{\left\langle V^{2}\right\rangle }{2\bar{V}}\]


A bar has Poisson arrivals and one member of staff serving. When there
are no customers at the bar, the staff member leaves the bar to check
on the kitchen. Assuming these checks are exponentially distributed
in length, with mean $\bar{V}$ and that customer service times are
exponentially distributed with mean $\bar{X}$ what is the average
waiting time int he queue?

Exponential standard deviation = $\frac{1}{\mu}$, mean$=\frac{1}{\mu}$.
So if mean is $\bar{V}$, standard deviation is $\bar{V}$ and variance
is $\bar{V}^{2}$. Thus second moment is $\left\langle V^{2}\right\rangle =2\bar{V}^{2}$.
Similarly for second moment of service time $\left\langle X^{2}\right\rangle =2\bar{X}^{2}$.
Defining $\rho=\lambda\bar{X}$ we have \[
\bar{W}=\frac{\lambda\bar{X}}{\left(1-\rho\right)}+\bar{V}=\frac{\rho}{\left(1-\rho\right)}+\bar{V}.\]
Deterministic vacations would have lead to \[
\bar{W}=\frac{\lambda\bar{X}}{\left(1-\rho\right)}+\frac{\bar{V}}{2}=\frac{\rho}{\left(1-\rho\right)}+\frac{\bar{V}}{2}.\]
 


\chapter{Putting Queues Together}

Consider the simple system involving two transmission lines in tandem.
Packet lengths are exponentially distributed, arrivals occur as a
Poisson process.

The first queue may be modeled as $M/M/1$. However the second queue
cannot be. This is because a large packet will typically experience
less delay at the second queue than a small one. 

\textbf{\emph{Put the detailed analysis from Bertsekas and Gallagher
in here.}}

This is a result of the second queue having a chance to clear while
the large packet is under transmission.

In Kleinrock's independence Approximation we simply assume that this
correlation does not exist.

Consider a general network with labelled nodes and links between these
nodes.

There are several packet streams in the network, each stream has a
rate of $x_{s}$. We define $f_{ij}\left(s\right)$ as the fraction
of packets from stream $s$ that cross the link between $i$ and $j$.
The rate associated with a link between node $i$ and $j$ is then
\begin{eqnarray*}
\lambda_{ij} & = & \sum_{s\textrm{ }}f_{ij}\left(s\right)x_{s}.\end{eqnarray*}
Kleinrock suggested that merging traffic streams on a transmission
line has the effect of restoring independence of arrival and service
times. The approach is to assume that each link can be treated as
an $M/M/1$ queue. 

Good approximation for 

\begin{enumerate}
\item arrivals which occur as a Poisson process 
\item exponentially distributed packets
\item densely connected networks 
\item moderate-heavy traffic.
\end{enumerate}
Given this assumption, from the $M/M/1$ queue we know that the average
number at each link is \[
\bar{N}_{ij}=\frac{\lambda_{ij}}{\mu_{ij}+\lambda_{ij}}\]
thus the average number in the entire system is\begin{eqnarray*}
\bar{N} & = & \sum_{ij}\bar{N}_{ij}\\
 & = & \sum_{ij}\frac{\lambda_{ij}}{\mu_{ij}+\lambda_{ij}}\end{eqnarray*}
average delay at each link is given by Little's theorem\[
\bar{T}_{ij}=\frac{1}{\mu_{ij}+\lambda_{ij}}\]

\chapter{Multiaccess Systems}

Statistical Multiplexing vs Time and Frequency division


\paragraph{Example 3.9 in Bertsekas \& Gallager}

Assume we have m statistically independent Poisson streams. Each has
arrival rate $\frac{\lambda}{m}$. Each has an average transmission
time $\bar{X}$. 

If we merge the Poisson streams together, through statistical multiplexing,
property of Poisson from Lecture 3\&4 tell us that they become a Poisson
stream with rate $\lambda$. Average delay, from last lecture will
be\[
\bar{T}=\frac{1}{\mu-\lambda}.\]
Now consider an alternative approach of providing each channel with
a separate circuit. This involves splitting our transmission line
into $m$ channels. Each will now have bandwidth at most $\frac{\mu}{m}$.

Delay in this system will now be\[
\bar{T}=\frac{1}{\frac{\mu}{m}-\frac{\lambda}{m}}=\frac{m}{\mu-\lambda}\]
or $m$ times larger than statistical multiplexing. 

Why does this happen?

Consider the situation where there is only one packet in the system.
In this case much of the bandwidth will be redundant.
